topic: Solid-state batteries for electric vehicles: technical challenges, leading electrolyte approaches and commercialization timeline

key_points.point: Solid-state cells swap the liquid electrolyte for a solid one and can use a lithium-metal anode (about 3,860 mAh/g versus about 372 for graphite), promising higher energy density.
The three main inorganic electrolyte families are sulfides, oxides and halides, plus polymers; sulfides and oxides are the most developed for automotive all-solid-state cells.

Sulfide electrolytes (e.g. argyrodite Li6PS5Cl, about 1 mS/cm) conduct ions well but are air-sensitive, can release H2S, and have a narrow electrochemical window and instability against lithium metal.

Oxide electrolytes such as garnet LLZO are stable and conductive (about 1e-3 to 1e-2 S/cm) but brittle, need high-temperature sintering and suffer high interfacial impedance and poor lithium wettability.
Polymer electrolytes are cheaper and technically easier to make but their performance lags liquid electrolytes; halides are a newer route with oxidation, moisture and indium-cost issues.

Core engineering challenge is the solid-solid interface: volume changes during cycling cause cracking and contact loss, so cells often need high stack pressure, which adds cost and lowers cell-level density.
Lithium dendrites can still penetrate solid electrolytes via cracks, grain boundaries and pores; high stiffness alone does not stop them, and sulfides show crack-first, dendrite-following failure.
Cost and manufacturing scale are major barriers: all-solid-state cells cost roughly CNY 3-5/Wh versus an industry target below CNY 2/Wh, and sulfide electrolyte output is only tens of tonnes.
Toyota's first solid-state EV target has repeatedly slipped; it now cites 2027-2028 (other sources say end of decade), with Idemitsu's electrolyte plant due in 2027.
Samsung SDI targets sulfide all-solid-state mass production from late 2027; QuantumScape's Eagle Line pilot started in 2026; BYD plans small-batch fitment in 2027.

Most 2026-2028 vehicle deployments are semi-solid or demonstration fleets; NIO's semi-solid pack was reportedly discontinued after a few hundred units, and test vehicles are a poor guide to production timing.
Forecasts see tiny all-solid-state volumes by 2028 (about 3.5 GWh) and real scale (>50 GWh/yr) only after 2030, with about 10% penetration by 2035 per one analyst.
